source: Dokic, Koso-Drljevic and Bilalic (2025) Past reflections, present insights: a systematic review and new empirical research into the WMC-Gf relationship (Intelligence 108, 101874)
finding: Repository record with the full English abstract. The review says evidence is mixed. Only Little et al. 2014 is named as a positive study. Named non-supportive studies: Burgoyne 2019, Salthouse 1993, Unsworth 2014, Unsworth and Engle 2005, Wiley 2011. The new test (N=543) used Operation, Reading and Symmetry Span and Raven APM items. No support for the capacity hypothesis by item difficulty, by rule-token count, or in SEM and latent growth curve models.
numbers: N=543 (non-Anglo-Saxon sample). 3 complex span tasks. Three analysis routes (item difficulty, rule tokens, SEM/LGCM) all null. Review study count and inclusion rule are NOT stated in the abstract.
quote: the majority of others did not observe a significant increase in correlation
limits: Abstract only; the PDF and the review table were not reachable (ScienceDirect blocked, the repository has no file). So the number of reviewed studies and how each was coded stay unknown. The repository lists the DOI as 10.1016/j.intell.2024.101874.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 is half closed: the pattern is known (mixed, majority null), the counts are not. Do not quote a study count. Use 'majority null, Little the main exception'.

source: Burgoyne, Hambrick and Altmann (2019) Is working memory capacity a causal factor in fluid intelligence? Psychonomic Bulletin & Review
finding: Independent test of the item-difficulty prediction with Raven items and two WMC measures: complex span and the k estimate from Visual Arrays. Neither WMC measure showed the predicted rise of correlation with item difficulty. Restriction of range in item scores did not explain the null.
numbers: Two WMC measures (complex span, visual arrays k). Sample size and slopes not read.
limits: Abstract only (read through Europe PMC). Numbers unknown. The Springer full text redirected to a login page.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: this is an independent check on Little 2014 with a different lab and a non-span WM task. It is still null. It argues the single positive result is not robust.

source: Little, Lewandowsky and Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better. Frontiers in Psychology (full text re-read)
finding: The paper holds an internal replication. The main study used RAPM and a four-task WM composite. A second study (Supplementary Material, not read) used the Standard Progressive Matrices (RSPM) in a new sample and replicated the rising slope; with a weaker WM measure the RSPM effect was reduced, not absent. Simulation: the item-wise slope rises with the population correlation (0.0002, 0.0006, 0.0009, 0.0013, 0.0015, 0.0016 for rho .1 to .9). Bootstrapped overall correlations .53, .23, .09 gave shrinking slopes.
numbers: 130 volunteers (95 female, mean age 21.12), two 1-hour sessions. Composite r with RAPM = .56. Slope .004, t(34)=2.87, p<.01, r2=.20. OSPAN alone: r=.36, slope t(34)=1.39, p>.05, r2=.05. Rule-token multilevel model: tokens beta=-0.10 (SE .005); WMC x tokens beta=.02. No novelty effect.
quote: the more difficult Raven's items indeed tax WMC more than the easier items
limits: Supplementary replication text not read. Same lab, same battery. The slope is small (.004 per item). The simulation assumes a bivariate normal link, which Frischkorn and Oberauer say makes any such test uninformative about capacity.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: one same-lab replication with a different Raven form exists, plus two later independent nulls (Burgoyne 2019, Dokic 2025). The positive result needs a strong overall WM-Gf correlation. Read any null together with the overall r.

source: Carpenter, Just and Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psychological Review 97, 404-431), as described in Little et al. 2014
finding: The original was not reachable (PsycNet page blank, no open copy). Little et al. describe it: people infer rules from a taxonomy (pairwise increments and decrements, distribution of 3, distribution of 2 as XOR, addition as OR, subtraction as AND). Two production-system models were compared. Number of rule tokens explained 57% of the variance in item accuracy. Distribution-of-2 items appear only late in the test, where accuracy is lowest.
numbers: 57% of item-accuracy variance from total rule tokens (via Little). Example items: 3 rule tokens (easy), 6 rule tokens (hard). Some items were excluded by Carpenter for technical reasons.
limits: Second-hand. Rule tokens and rule type are confounded with item position in the test. The 57% is across items, not across people. The goal-management claims in the original are NOT verified.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for the original. Safe use: rule tokens do track average item accuracy (57%), which is why rule count is a tempting budget rule. The item-wise WM results (K04) show that is not the same as WM load.

source: Kyllonen and Christal (1990) Reasoning ability is (little more than) working-memory capacity?! Intelligence 14, 389-433
finding: Not opened. Crossref gives the title and no abstract. Later papers cite it only as showing a strong WM-reasoning link. The latent correlations .80 to .88 in the gap list could not be checked.
limits: ScienceDirect returned 403. The value from memory stays unverified.
agent_relevance: Do not cite .80 to .88 as checked. Use the later latent range (.74 to .96) that we did read (K09).

source: Patil, Kumar, Sinha and Mandal (2026) Beyond Accuracy: Diagnosing Algebraic Reasoning Failures in LLMs Across Nine Complexity Dimensions (arXiv 2604.06799)
finding: Seven instruction-tuned models from 8B to 235B parameters. Each complexity factor was varied alone. The working-memory factor (parallel branches) collapses between 20 and 30 branches for every model, with no gradient and no recovery. Qwen3 235B and Llama 3 8B fail at identical thresholds. Other factors do differ by model (counting load; tree depth, where Qwen3 235B keeps 17% at depth 8).
numbers: 7 models, 8B to 235B. Plateau at 100% from 2 to 12 branches; sharp drop from 15 to 25 branches; 0% by 30 and through 200. Operator-difficulty ordering Spearman .863 on Qwen-2.5-7B across two runs.
quote: working memory is the dominant scale-invariant bottleneck
limits: Instruction-tuned models, probably without long reasoning. Preprint under review. Branch count is an item-demand axis, but nothing is correlated with a capacity score.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (partial): the closest size sweep found. The demand threshold did NOT move with model size, unlike the human-style prediction that the curve peak shifts with mean capacity. It fits a fixed architecture or format limit, not a graded capacity. Run the same branch sweep on our agent with and without scratch notes at equal tokens.

source: Ravulapalli and Chadha (2026) In-Context Binding Capacity in Language Models (arXiv 2609.30634)
finding: Measures how many variable-value bindings a model recalls before recall falls halfway to chance (K50). For 12 models up to 3B, K50 = c * N^0.82 (R2=.73). A threshold sweep over 30 open models up to 12B shows an 8x range tied to pretraining recipe. The Pythia ladder holds k between 3 and 6 from 410M to 12B (29x parameters). Qwen2.5 goes 3, 10, 24 (censored at the ceiling), 16 at 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B. The recipe effect disappears after controlling for scale in the continuous curves (coefficient +0.123, CI -0.521 to 0.363).
numbers: 12 models <=3B (continuous curves), 30 models <=12B (threshold sweep). AUC exponent +0.329 on log parameters. Collapse slope is tightly coupled to K50 (r=-0.837 in logs).
limits: Static recall of bindings, not reasoning. No capacity-by-demand interaction on reasoning items. Preprint; few modern models in the fit.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a real, measurable LLM capacity that varies with size and recipe. It is a candidate capacity axis for an LLM version of the Frischkorn design, but the study never links it to reasoning item difficulty. It also warns that recipe, not parameter count, can set capacity.

source: Ravulapalli and Chadha (2026) In-Context Binding Capacity: interference results (arXiv 2609.30634)
finding: Distractor tokens (interference) lower measured binding recall. Whether the damage tracks capacity is not settled: the ceiling falls with distractors, and its association with capacity is inconclusive. Collapse rates do not follow the capacity ranking.
numbers: Spearman -0.473, p=0.142 (ceiling drop vs capacity). Spearman +0.20, p=0.56, n=11 (collapse rate vs capacity).
limits: Small n (11 to 12 models). Retrieval task only.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: capacity and interference look like separate dials in LLMs. Test them separately (distractor-length sweep versus load sweep) and do not file all failure under capacity.

source: Ghaffari et al. (2026) Context Poisoning as Extreme-Value Attention Interference in Long-Context Language Models (arXiv 2609.22101)
finding: Theory plus two controlled tests. Under a softmax retrieval model, holding accuracy requires the evidence margin to grow with log of the effective distractor count (not raw length). Retrieval accuracy falls as embedded hard negatives rise. Same-format distractors cause the largest drop at fixed context length. Retrieval gating helps only if recall is kept.
numbers: Fitted exponential decay R2=0.74 (exploratory). Accuracy drops between N=100 and N=300 hard negatives, then plateaus through N=1000 on a production model.
limits: Preprint from an industry team; one production model; exploratory fit. Retrieval, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: supports an interference account of long-context failure that differs from a capacity count. For our agent: filter or compress distractor context (S2) before adding tokens, and measure by distractor count, not total length.

source: Evaluating Relational Reasoning in LLMs with REL (arXiv 2604.12176), tool-use and in-context sections
finding: Giving a model a chemistry toolkit (RDKit) on the isomer-listing task did not remove the decline with relational complexity. In-context examples raised completion at low load but kept the task ordering (C1 77.0%, +6.6; C2 43.3%, +3.4; C3 32.7%, +6.0). Opus 4.5 recall 0.341, 0.313, 0.253 as observed molecules rise from under 20 to 40 or more.
limits: The tool arm is a different model (GPT-5.4) from the no-tool GPT-5.2, so it is not a paired test. Tools only parsed molecules; the model still had to hold the whole enumeration. No output-length log.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: decomposition by code helped parsing but not the bottleneck. Contrast d11, where code fully fixed an indexing step. Code helps when it does the binding itself, not when the model still carries the joint set.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (arXiv 2404.13070)
finding: Reply to critiques of Webb 2023. On shuffled-alphabet letter-string analogies, GPT-4 alone does worse than people. GPT-4 with code execution reaches human level, and it chose to write code itself to turn letters into indices. 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule, against 39% for humans.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Human vs GPT-4: P=8.9e-13. Human vs GPT-4 + code: P=0.496. Interval-size effect: humans P=1.5e-11, GPT-4 P<2e-16, GPT-4 + code P=0.066.
limits: Authors of the original claim. The code arm is a different model build. Counting and indexing was the identified weak step.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: code decomposition (O3) restored human-level accuracy when the failing step was exact indexing. Log which step fails before choosing code or text.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (arXiv 2506.09250), details read
finding: Critique of Shojaee et al. The collapse at large Tower of Hanoi sizes matches output-token limits. River Crossing was scored as failure on instances that are mathematically unsolvable. Asking for a Lua function instead of the full move list gave very high accuracy at N=15 in under 5,000 tokens for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3 and Gemini 2.5.
numbers: N=15 disks, four model families, under 5,000 tokens. River Crossing unsolvable for N>5 with boat capacity 3 (as the comment states).
limits: Self-labelled preliminary. No per-model accuracy table. It shows the collapse was partly format, not that complexity never matters.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: output length is a real confound. Before reading any collapse as a capacity limit, log truncation and test a compact representation (code) at the same token budget.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (arXiv 2604.10739)
finding: Budget-forcing sweep of reasoning length on R1-32B and s1-32B. Returns shrink at high budgets and turn negative; models drop correct answers. The best budget depends on difficulty: easy items peak early (about 1.0 to 1.5K tokens), hard items keep gaining to about 7.5 to 8K. A tight cap loses hard items first; a large budget hurts easy items.
numbers: MATH-500 optimal budget 1.0K (Level 1) to 7.5K (Level 5). AIME R1-32B accuracy 41.4% at 2K, 55.6% at 10K, 53.1% at 16K; flip ratio 7.55 [6.12, 9.24] at 16K. Of 80 negative flips checked by hand, 67.5% were true overthinking and 12.5% artefact.
limits: Two distilled reasoning models, math only. Budget forcing may itself distort. Not a Raven task, no human control. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the LLM analogue of Chuderski's time pressure points the same way: a tight cap loses hard items first. Set the token budget by difficulty class (G12) and run a cap-by-difficulty grid. The Colom non-replication has no LLM counterpart.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using Counterfactual Tasks to Evaluate the Generality of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models (arXiv 2402.08955)
finding: Follow-up on Webb 2023 letter-string analogies. Humans stay high on permuted and symbolic alphabets. GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop sharply as the alphabet is permuted more. Models pass a comprehension check, so the drop is not only misunderstanding. Human accuracy on the original problems was higher than in Webb's own sample.
numbers: Humans: 1,876 samples, overall accuracy about 0.75 (95% CI .734 to .773). The three GPT models score 0.35 to 0.49 overall (table labels are scrambled in the PDF text, so the model-to-number mapping is uncertain).
limits: Pre-reasoning-model GPTs (2023-24). Webb's reply (d11) shows code execution closes much of the gap. Not a unique-rule test.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 (partial): the Webb 2023 results do not carry over to counterfactual alphabets for plain GPTs. No test of the unique-rule effect on current reasoning models or on image Raven items was found.

source: MaRs-VQA authors (2025) What is the Visual Cognition Gap between Humans and Multimodal LLMs? (arXiv 2406.10424, COLM 2025), difficulty appendix
finding: Image matrix items graded 1 to 5 by the number and type of changing attributes. GPT-4o with chain of thought drops from easy to hard, but not in a clean line. Few-shot examples lifted GPT-4o from 34% to 36%, with no gain at 5 shots. The authors name vision, not language, as the main bottleneck.
numbers: GPT-4o + CoT by level (items 90, 96, 84, 72, 138): 57.78% at Level 1 and 21.74% at Level 5; the middle levels sit near 19% to 27% (the level-to-number mapping in the extracted table is scrambled).
limits: One model; attribute-count levels are a rule-count style proxy. Table layout damaged in extraction, so only the endpoints are safe.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and K04: attribute count gives a large easy-hard gap but a non-monotone middle. This supports measuring difficulty empirically, not by count. Image perception is also a separate error source.

source: Ding et al. (2024/2025) Easy2Hard-Bench: Standardized Difficulty Labels for Profiling LLM Performance and Generalization (arXiv 2409.18433)
finding: Difficulty fitted by IRT from LLM leaderboard responses was checked against human pairwise judgments of which item is harder. It agrees well with people on GSM8K and much less on ARC and Winogrande. GPT-4 as a difficulty judge agrees with IRT difficulty poorly outside GSM8K.
numbers: IRT vs human matching accuracy 0.942 (GSM8K), 0.737 (ARC), 0.734 (Winogrande). IRT vs GPT-4 matching 0.836, 0.616, 0.597. Spearman IRT vs GPT-4 rank: 0.612, 0.218, 0.164.
limits: Fitted over many LLMs pooled, so it measures average-model difficulty. It does not compare IRT with rule-count or relational-complexity predictors. The paper's two tables report slightly different GPT-4 vs human numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 (partial): fitted difficulty is a valid ordering but not equally good across domains, and an LLM judge cannot replace fitting. No study was found that tests rule count against fitted IRT on matrices. Run that comparison on our own bank.

source: Ge et al. (2026) Agent Psychometrics: Task-Level Performance Prediction in Agentic Coding Benchmarks (arXiv 2604.00594, COLM 2026)
finding: IRT with task features predicts which tasks agents solve. Agent ability splits additively into an LLM part and a scaffold part, which allows prediction for unseen LLM-scaffold pairs. Task features read by an LLM judge beat the plain baseline but stay below the oracle IRT fit.
numbers: Held-out task AUC-ROC, LLM-judge features: SWE-bench Verified .840, SWE-bench Pro .743, GSO .778, Terminal-Bench 2.0 .794. Baseline .718, .656, .718, .732. Oracle .945, .918, .916, .932. Combined features .841, .763, .787, .792.
limits: Coding agents, not reasoning matrices. Features are LLM-judged text descriptions, not a count of rules.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10: a structure-based predictor closes part of the gap to the oracle but does not match it. The scaffold effect is separately estimable (additive). Use fitted difficulty for the budget and treat counts as extra features.

source: Search log: arXiv listing sweep for a model-size by item-demand design (Raven, relational complexity, IRT, scaling)
finding: Listing searches returned 15 Raven-LLM papers, 1 relational-complexity paper (REL) and 19 IRT-LLM difficulty papers. None correlates a capacity score with item-wise demand across several capacity levels, which is the Frischkorn and Oberauer design. The web search quota ran out during this pass and the arXiv API was rate-limited, so the sweep is not exhaustive.
numbers: Raven + language models: 15 hits (2019-2026). IRT + LLM benchmark difficulty: 19 hits. Relational complexity + LLM: 1 relevant hit.
limits: Absence of evidence from title and abstract listings only. Not proof that no such study exists.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 10: no ready-made study. We would have to run the design ourselves, with several capacity levels (model, context length, scratch notes) at equal tokens.
